take: Trump’s narrower-than-expected Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire, reportedly covering only refineries, matters most for crude and products because it leaves the broader supply-disruption premium intact whilst the US has simultaneously lifted sanctions on Russian diesel for six months under General License 135 until 7 April 2027, a bearish offset for gasoil and distillate cracks. The tanker war spreading deeper into the Gulf, with a fully laden VLCC struck off the UAE and another tanker hit in the Strait of Hormuz, is the second theme, and it transmits directly into freight: supertanker rates have already soared to record highs as the Iran conflict reshuffles trade routes and ties up tonnage in inefficient, lengthy voyages, with Clarksons’ cross-sector ClarkSea Index up 12% in a week to an unprecedented $84,951 a day. On flows and inventories, the IEA’s additional 100 million barrel release of diesel, gasoline and crude, alongside an SPR at just 283 million barrels at end-September — the lowest since October 1982 — risks draining the world’s last supply cushion, whilst China plans to resume refined fuel exports. The cross-market link to watch is bunker versus gasoil: the US diesel sanctions waiver pulls Russian barrels into the pool just as Singapore’s SIBCON delegates gather, capping marine fuel upside even as record tanker earnings and a 7.7 magnitude Panama earthquake — with canal transits continuing pending inspections — keep tonne-mile and routing risk elevated. In the next 24 hours, watch Hurricane Isaias landfall on the Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday for production shut-ins, any widening of the ceasefire terms beyond refineries, and whether the Panama Canal authority’s inspections disrupt transits.
